rewriteLast.title: Chapter 5 · The Grand Birthday Feast
rewriteLast.artPrompt: a great castle courtyard festival at dusk with long tables of farm families eating and laughing, garlands and lanterns strung between stone walls, a small curly-haired boy in velvet waving from a shaggy pony, a tall old earl rising with a raised glass, fireworks beginning in a violet sky, joyful warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last came Cedric's birthday, and the Earl gave the grandest feast the county had ever seen. Every tenant for miles came to the castle with wives and children and grandmothers. They came in carts and on foot, in their Sunday best. Long tables stood in the courtyard. Garlands swung between the stone walls. The kitchens roasted and steamed from morning till night. The tenants came in their Sunday best, and their Sunday best had been brushed and mended for a week. Never, said the oldest men, had such a day been seen on the Earl's land.

Cedric rode his shaggy pony up and down the lines, waving until his arm ached. There were games for the children, races for the boys, and toys under the trees. And Dearest came too, at the Earl's own invitation, in her best dress, and sat near the Earl's great chair. The old Earl watched everything from under his fierce eyebrows — and nobody could remember his face ever looking less cross. Once, when a small boy dropped his plate, the whole courtyard froze. But the Earl only laughed, and had the plate filled again. The cheering that followed could be heard all the way at the lodge.
The grandest feast the county had ever seen, with the little lord on his pony.
Question for you: The Earl once kept Cedric's mother far away from the castle. Why do you think he asked her to the feast now?

Then, just as the fireworks began, the Earl stood up before all the people. A hush went over the courtyard. He raised his glass, and his old voice shook a little. "To my grandson," he said, "the little Lord Fauntleroy — and to his mother, the finest lady in England."

The cheers rolled and rolled, like waves coming in. Dearest smiled with tears in her eyes, and Cedric glowed like a small lantern in his velvet suit. And high above the castle, the first fireworks bloomed and bloomed against the darkening sky.

chapters.title: Chapter 6 · The Earl Asks Forgiveness
chapters.artPrompt: a tall old earl standing hat-in-hand at the rose-covered door of a small cozy lodge where a gentle young woman listens with kind eyes, morning light over the garden, servants peeping from castle windows far away, tender quiet mood, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The morning after the feast, the Earl did a thing nobody in the castle could quite believe. He ordered his carriage and rode out, all alone, to the little lodge where Dearest lived. The servants watched from the windows. Nobody dared to say a single word.

Dearest opened the door herself, surprised. The Earl stood on her step, tall and stiff, holding his hat in his two hands. For the first time in anyone's memory, the proudest man in England looked unsure of himself. "Madam," he said, "I have done you a great wrong." His voice was not used to saying such words, and it stumbled. But his eyes were steady, and his hat was held out like an offering.
The proudest man in England, hat in hand, at a cottage door.
Talk together: The Earl was the proudest man in England, and saying sorry was the hardest thing he ever did. Why is sorry sometimes the bravest word of all?

"I was proud and unkind, when you were only good," he went on. "I kept you from your son, and my grandson from his mother. Can you forgive an old man?" Dearest looked at him a long moment. Then she held out her hand, and her smile was as gentle as morning. "Cedric loves you," she said. "And he is nearly always right about people." The Earl held the small hand in his great one for a moment. It was as if it were something he had almost lost. Then he bowed — actually bowed, at a cottage door — and drove back up the hill a different man.

That evening the Earl told Cedric the news, trying very hard to look cross about something. "Your mother will come and live here, in the castle, with us." Cedric gave a shout of joy that rang down three corridors. Then he hugged the old Earl with both arms, and did not let go for a long, long time. The maids heard the shout three corridors away, and smiled at their work without knowing why.

chapters.title: Chapter 7 · Home at the Castle
chapters.artPrompt: a great castle hearth at evening with an old earl in his chair, a gentle young mother knitting, and a small curly-haired boy telling a story with both hands raised, firelight on stone walls and banners, a shaggy dog asleep on the hearth, cozy warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: So Dearest came to live at the castle, and the great gray stone place was never the same again. Her rooms filled with flowers. Her laugh was heard in the halls. And every evening the three of them sat by the big fireplace — the Earl, Dearest, and the little lord between them. Dearest put fresh flowers on the great table every day. The Earl pretended not to notice, and noticed every single one.

Cedric still told his stories of Mr. Hobbs and the apple turnovers, and the Earl still listened, grumbling on principle and missing not one word. "Tell me about the shoemaker boy again," the Earl would say. And Cedric told it all, from the very beginning, as if it were brand new. Sometimes Dearest read aloud instead, and the fire popped, and the oldest room in the house felt young again.
Stories by the great fire, with the whole family together at last.
New word: tenant - a person who farms or lives on a lord's land and pays rent for it. The Earl had hundreds of them, and Cedric knew them all by name.

The tenants saw everything, and told each other the news from farm to farm. The Earl walked in the village now. He lifted his hat to grandmothers. He asked after sick children and new calves. "The little lord has tamed him," the people said. But the maids, who saw the most, said it was the other way about. It was the strangest thing the county had ever seen, and the county had seen a good many strange things by then.

At night the halls glowed with firelight from end to end. The castle had been the proudest, coldest house in all the county. Now it was the warmest — and everyone knew the small reason why, and loved him for it. Even the portraits on the stairs looked less stern, said Cedric — though that, admitted the Earl, might have been the candlelight.

chapters.title: Chapter 8 · Letters Across the Sea
chapters.artPrompt: a small curly-haired boy at a castle desk writing a long letter by candlelight with a satisfied old earl reading over his shoulder, sealing wax and a packet of letters tied with string, rain on the tall window, warm storybook illustration

blocks.text: Far away in New York, two friends of the little lord had not been forgotten. The Earl sent Dick enough money to open a boot-black stand of his own. It came with fine new brushes and a sign with gold letters. And Cedric wrote letters by the yard. He wrote about the castle, and the pony, and the fireworks. He also wrote the exact number of stairs, which he had counted twice to be sure.

"Dear Mr. Hobbs," the letters began, "I am still a lord, and grandfather says you saved the whole family, and we are much obliged. Grandfather is much kinder now. He laughs — truly he does. I am not telling stories. You can ask anybody." The letters went off in a fat packet. Dick's was tied in red string, because red string was the correct honor for a particular friend.
Long letters for New York, written by candlelight with the Earl reading over his shoulder.
Kindness travels farther than you think. A good deed done in a small grocery store once helped save an old family in England.

And back across the sea came a great box from Mr. Hobbs, with presents for everybody and a letter full of news. Three cheers had been given in the store the day the good news arrived, he wrote. The clerks had stood on the counter to do it. Dick wrote too, on splendid new paper. His stand was the smartest in the city, and every boot he shone was shone like a lord's. He had bought a sign with gold letters on it. His first customer was the mayor, who declared it the finest shine in the state.

The Earl read the letters aloud at supper, which surprised everybody the first time and nobody after that. "Your friends," he said, "are honest men. That is worth more than titles." Cedric beamed at him across the table. He thought so too. After supper they planned another letter to New York together. For once it was the Earl who suggested most of the kind things to put in it.

chapters.title: Chapter 9 · The Gladdest Home in England
chapters.artPrompt: an old earl, a young mother, and a growing boy walking together along a castle garden path at golden evening, roses and clipped yew hedges, the castle towers warm in the sunset behind them, peaceful joyful storybook illustration

blocks.text: The seasons turned, and the castle grew used to its happiness, the way a house grows used to music. Cedric grew taller, and rode faster, and learned his lessons — most of them. He never once forgot to be kind. It was simply the way he was made. He still told baseball stories on Sunday evenings. The Earl understood about one word in ten, and pretended it was plenty.

The old Earl still grumbled on principle, but nobody was fooled anymore. Kind things got done all over the county now — quietly, before anyone could even ask. By the next day the Earl pretended he had forgotten every one of them. The tenants smiled, and let him pretend. Cottage roofs got mended. The school got new benches. If a haycart stuck, there was somehow always a fine horse standing near, and nobody could ever say whose.
Evening walks in the garden, with the warm castle towers behind.
Question for you: One small boy changed a whole castle - not with gold or a grand title, but with a kind word and a brave, honest heart. What small kindness could you do this week?

On summer evenings the three of them walked in the garden together — the Earl, Dearest, and Cedric between them. Cedric told them both the news of the village. The old man's face had lost its last crossness for good. The coldest house in the county had become the gladdest home in England. Travelers who passed by the park wall began to slow their horses, just to look. They said you could tell the castle by its windows, because there were flowers in every one of them.

And it had all begun with a small boy who said good morning to a cross old gentleman. He said it as if the old man were just a grandfather. Which, of course, was exactly what he was. Kindness, Cedric had found, is catching. And nobody, least of all the Earl, ever wanted to be cured.
